sections.h2: Who records deeds in Cook County
sections.html:
The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division records, stores and maintains land records for the county, including deeds and mortgages. Its office hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the last customer is accepted at 4:45 p.m.

Anyone can look up recorded documents in the Clerk's search tool by PIN, grantor, grantee and other indexed details. The Clerk also runs a legal help desk where a volunteer attorney can discuss recording questions, a process to petition to strike unlawful restrictive covenants from old property records, and an e-certify service that verifies electronic certified copies.

  • Search recorded land records by PIN or by party name.
  • Review the Clerk's document requirements before you go.
  • Use the fee schedule to estimate cost, since the final fee is set after the document is inspected.

A deed is priced as Document Class 1 at $107 under the schedule that took effect April 1, 2024. The office no longer prices documents as standard or non-standard, and nearly every recording now falls into one of seven document classes.

Any document priced at $107 or more includes a $55 county recording fee, a $23 GIS fee, a $10 document storage fee, an $18 State Rental Housing Support fee and a $1 non-government filer fee. Filers not subject to the state support fee are priced $19 lower.

sections.h2: Why the Clerk will not quote a fee by phone
sections.html:
The final fee can change once staff inspect the document, so quotes are not given over the phone. Bring cash or a credit card, or wait to fill in the amount on a check until you meet a cashier.

Copies have their own fees: $55 for a paper certified copy, $65 for a certified digital PDF, $27.50 for a non-certified paper copy and $5 for a non-certified download. Copies paid for online carry a 2.10% credit card fee. A DD-214 military discharge, including additional certified copies, is recorded free.

sections.h2: What a Cook County deed must contain
sections.html:
Every real estate document needs certain items, and deeds need a few more. Missing items are the common reason a recording is turned away.

  • The property must be in Cook County and the document must relate to real estate.
  • Mail-to and prepared-by names and addresses, the common address and the PIN.
  • A legal description, legible type of at least 10 point, and notarization where required.
  • For deeds: grantor and grantee names and addresses, and a completed MyDec for the state and county tax stamps.
  • Municipal real estate transfer tax information, and a grantor and grantee affidavit when the deed is an exempt transaction.

Exempt deeds carry exemption language. The Clerk's example reads "Exempt under Real Estate Transfer Law Tax 35 ILCS 200/31-45 sub par ___ and Cook County Ord. 93-O-27 par ___," followed by a signature and date. Mortgages need the state Anti-Predatory Lending certificate as the first page. Plats must be between 8 1/2 by 14 inches and 30 by 36 inches, submitted as an original with three copies.

Illinois taxes the transfer of title, and the county collects it through revenue stamps sold by the Department of Revenue. If the home stays subject to an existing mortgage, only the owner's equity counts in the tax base, provided the deed or trust agreement says so on its face. The statutes are 35 ILCS 200/31-1 to 31-70.

State law lets a county add a tax of 25 cents per $500 of value, and a home rule municipality may add its own. With that layering, the amount due on a Cook County sale depends on the municipality where the house stands. Ask the Clerk or your title company for the stamps and local tax due on your deed.

  • Buyer and seller complete Form PTAX-203, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, filed in the county where the property sits.
  • Form PTAX-203-A is the supplement for non-residential property sold for more than $1 million.
  • Cook County asks for the MyDec filing before it will accept a deed.

The Clerk's Property Fraud Unit works on forged and fraudulent filings. Fraudsters can target homes without a mortgage and file forged documents with the recorder. Once a document is recorded, the owner must petition the court at personal expense to remove it, and selling or refinancing may be impossible until that is resolved.

The Clerk offers a free Property Fraud Alert that calls or emails an owner whenever a document is recorded against the property, including the property of a loved one. An owner who receives an alert can contact the Property Fraud Unit, and staff will research the problem and coordinate with law enforcement where indicated.

sections.h2: Other documents recorded around a sale
sections.html:
A sale often involves more than the deed. The Clerk also records releases of mortgage, assignments, mechanic's liens, lis pendens notices, judgments, contracts, powers of attorney and transfer on death instruments, each with its own checklist.

  • Releases and assignments need the previous recorded document number in addition to the standard items.
  • Powers of attorney and transfer on death instruments need a notarized signature.
  • Judgments need a certified copy, or the original with the judge's original signature.
  • A lis pendens must be signed by the party or an attorney.

If a mortgage payoff is part of your closing, ask the lender or title company when the release will be recorded, and keep the recorded document number for your file. A corrective recording affidavit needs the signatures of every party to the original document.

sections.h2: Getting ready to record after a sale
sections.html:
In most sales the title company prepares the package and sends it in, so your job is to supply clean information. Check the spelling of every name against the old deed, confirm the PIN and common address, and tell the title company where the buyer wants mail sent. If you are a cash seller closing quickly, ask the title company how it will record the deed and when, since a recorded deed is what finishes the transfer in the land records.

After recording, search the PIN in the Clerk's tool to confirm the deed and any release of your old mortgage appear. A missing release is easier to chase soon after closing than months later. If you ever see a recording you do not recognize, sign up for the Property Fraud Alert.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Cook County?
faqs.a: With the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division. Hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the last customer is accepted at 4:45 p.m. Recorded documents can be searched by PIN, grantor or grantee.

faqs.q: What is the recording fee for a Cook County deed?
faqs.a: The posted fee for a deed is $107. Documents not subject to the state rental housing support fee are priced $19 lower. The Clerk cannot give fee quotes by phone.

faqs.q: Can I record a Cook County deed by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. Recording by mail with return is $5 per document. The deed must still meet the document requirements, including the PIN, legal description and a completed MyDec.

faqs.q: What does a certified copy of a Cook County deed cost?
faqs.a: A paper certified copy is $55 and a certified digital PDF is $65. A non-certified paper copy is $27.50, and a non-certified download is $5. Online card payments add a 2.10% fee.

faqs.q: What is MyDec for Cook County deeds?
faqs.a: MyDec is the state's online system for the transfer declaration and tax stamps. The deed requirements call for a completed MyDec, and buyer and seller complete the PTAX-203 declaration.
